name: Scopa
description: Scopa is an Italian fishing card game where players capture table cards by matching rank or sum; points for sweeps, most cards, coins suit, sette bello and prime. First to 11+ points wins.

content.text: Scopa is an Italian fishing card game where players capture table cards by matching rank or sum; points for sweeps, most cards, coins suit, sette bello and prime. First to 11+ points wins.

Country/Region of Origin: Italy
Time Period: 18th century (popular in Naples); roots in 15th-century Spanish games in Naples
Historical Development: Evolved from Spanish games Primero and Scarabucion in Naples port area; one of three major national card games in Italy with Briscola and Tresette
Cultural Significance: Popular social and family game in Italy; spread to Argentina, Brazil, and former Italian colonies via diaspora

Minimum Players: 2
Maximum Players: 6
Optimal Players: 2 or 4 (partnerships)
Partnerships: Optional for 4 or 6 players

Type: 40-card Italian or stripped 52-card deck (no 8s, 9s, 10s). Suits: coins, cups, swords, batons (Latin) or diamonds, hearts, clubs, spades (French). Ranks: King=10, Horse/Queen=9, Jack=8, 7–2 face value, Ace=1.
Number of Decks: 1
Jokers: Not included

Three cards to each player, then four cards face up to the table; deal one at a time. After each round of three plays, deal three more to each player (no new table cards). Direction: counter-clockwise with 3+ players.

items.text: Asso Pigliatutto: Playing an Ace captures all table cards (and scores a scopa) unless an Ace is on the table, in which case only the Ace is captured. Ace on empty table stays on table.
Scopa d'Assi: Like Asso Pigliatutto except capturing all cards with an Ace does not count as a scopa. Often played with four players (Scopone-style) with 9 or 10 cards each.
Scopa di Quindici: Capture only when the played card plus captured card(s) sum to 15 (e.g. play 4 to take 4+5+6). Popular in Argentina and Brazil. Some versions also allow equal-value capture.
